{{Short description|Theory that logical truth exists independent of human ideas}}
In [[logic]] and [[philosophy]], '''anti-psychologism''' (sometimes associated with  '''logical objectivism'''<ref>Dermot Moran, Rodney K. B. Parker (eds.), ''Studia Phaenomenologica: Vol. XV / 2015 – Early Phenomenology'', Zeta Books, 2016, p. 75: "Husserl was an exponent of logical objectivism and an opponent of logical psychologism".</ref> and, in stronger forms, with '''logical realism'''<ref>{{Interlanguage link multi|Edgar Morscher|de}} (1972), "Von Bolzano zu Meinong: Zur Geschichte des logischen Realismus." In: Rudolf Haller (ed.), ''Jenseits von Sein und Nichtsein: Beiträge zur Meinong-Forschung'', Graz, pp. 69–102.</ref><ref>Penelope Rush, "Logical Realism", in: Penelope Rush (ed.), ''The Metaphysics of Logic'', Cambridge University Press, 2014, pp. 13–31.</ref>) is the [[theory]] that [[logical truth]] does not depend upon the contents of human ideas, but exists independent of human ideas.

==Overview<!--'Psychologism dispute' redirects here-->==
The anti-psychologistic treatment of logic originated in the works of [[Immanuel Kant]] and [[Bernard Bolzano]].<ref>[http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/bolzano/ Bernard Bolzano (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)]; ''[[Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]'' (1998): "Ryle, Gilbert (1900-76)."</ref>

The concept of logical objectivism or anti-psychologism was further developed by [[Johannes Rehmke]] (founder of [[Greifswald objectivism]])<ref>Nikolay Milkov, ''Early Analytic Philosophy and the German Philosophical Tradition'', London: Bloomsbury, 2020, p. 157.</ref> and [[Gottlob Frege]] (founder of [[logicism]] the most famous anti-psychologist in the [[philosophy of mathematics]]), and has been the center of an important debate in early [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]] and [[analytical philosophy]]. Frege's work was likely influenced by Bolzano.<ref>Sundholm, B. G., [https://openaccess.leidenuniv.nl/handle/1887/10421 "When, and why, did Frege read Bolzano?"], LOGICA Yearbook 1999, 164–174 (2000).</ref>

Elements of anti-psychologism in the [[historiography of philosophy]] can be found in the work of the members of the 1830s [[speculative theist]] movement of [[Christian Hermann Weisse]],<ref>William R. Woodward, ''Hermann Lotze: An Intellectual Biography'', Cambridge University Press, 2015, pp. 74–5.</ref> the late work of [[Hermann Lotze]],<ref>{{cite SEP |url-id=hermann-lotze |title=Hermann Lotze |last=Sullivan |first=David}}</ref> and the work of [[neo-Kantians]] [[Alois Riehl]] and [[Paul Natorp]].<ref>[https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/psychologism/#HusAntArg Psychologism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy): "Husserl's Antipsychologistic Arguments"]</ref>

The '''psychologism dispute'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> ({{langx|de|Psychologismusstreit}})<ref>Matthias Rath, ''Der Psychologismusstreit in der deutschen Philosophie'', 1994</ref> in 19th-century German-speaking philosophy is closely related to the contemporary [[internalism and externalism]] debate in [[epistemology]]; [[psychologism]] is often construed as a kind of internalism (the thesis that no fact about the world can provide reasons for action independently of desires and beliefs) and anti-psychologism as a kind of externalism (the thesis that reasons are to be identified with objective features of the world).<ref>Giuseppina D'Oro, [https://www.academia.edu/241389/Collingwood_Psychologism_and_Internalism "Collingwood, psychologism and internalism,"] ''European Journal of Philosophy'' '''12'''(2):163–177 (2004): "internalism is often associated with psychologism".</ref>

Psychologism was defended by [[Theodor Lipps]], [[Gerardus Heymans]], [[Wilhelm Wundt]], [[Wilhelm Jerusalem]], [[Christoph von Sigwart]], [[Theodor Elsenhans]], and [[Benno Erdmann]].<ref>[https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/psychologism/#ExaPsyRea Psychologism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy): "Examples of Psychologistic Reasoning"]</ref>

[[Edmund Husserl]] was another important proponent of anti-psychologism, and this trait passed on to other phenomenologists, such as [[Martin Heidegger]], whose doctoral thesis was meant to be a refutation of psychologism. They shared the argument that, because the proposition "no-p is a not-p" is not [[logical equivalence|logically equivalent]] to "It is thought that 'no-p is a not-p'", psychologism does not logically stand.

[[Charles Sanders Peirce]]—whose fields included logic, philosophy, and experimental psychology<ref>Peirce (sometimes with [[Joseph Jastrow]]) investigated the [[Bayesian probability|probability judgments]] of experimental subjects, pioneering [[decision analysis]]. He and Jastrow wrote "On Small Differences in Sensation", ''Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences'' (1885), 3, 73–83, presented 17 October 1884, reprinted in [[Charles Sanders Peirce bibliography#CP|Collected Papers]] v. 7, paragraphs 21–35. ''Classics in the History of Psychology''. [http://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Peirce/small-diffs.htm Eprint].</ref>—could also be considered a critic of psychologism in logic.<ref>Peirce attacked the idea, held by some logicians at that time, that rationality rests on a feeling of logicality, rather than on fact. See the first of Peirce's 1903 [[Charles Sanders Peirce bibliography#Lectures by Peirce|Lowell Institute Lectures]] "What Makes a Reasoning Sound?", ''[[Charles Sanders Peirce bibliography#EP|Essential Peirce]]'' v. 2, pp. 242–257. See also the portion of Peirce's 1902 ''Minute Logic'' published in ''[[Charles Sanders Peirce bibliography#CP|Collected Papers]]'' v. 2 (1931), paragraphs 18–19 and 39–43. Peirce held that mathematical and philosophical logics [[Classification of the sciences (Peirce)|precede]] psychology as a special science and that they do not depend on it for principles.</ref>

==The return of psychologism==
{{See also|Cognitive science|Naturalized epistemology}}
Psychologism is not widely held amongst logicians today, but something like it has some high-profile defenders especially among those who do research at the intersection of logic and [[cognitive science]], for example [[Dov Gabbay]] and [[John Woods (logician)|John Woods]], who concluded that "whereas mathematical logic must eschew psychologism, the new logic cannot do without it".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |author1-link=Dov Gabbay |last2=Woods |first2=John |author2-link=John Woods (logician) |date=March 2001 |title=The New Logic |journal=Logic Journal of the IGPL |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=141–174 |doi=10.1093/jigpal/9.2.141 |url=http://www3.oup.co.uk/igpl/Volume_09/Issue_02/pdf/Gabbay.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050516003510/http://www3.oup.co.uk/igpl/Volume_09/Issue_02/pdf/Gabbay.pdf |archive-date=2005-05-16 |url-status=dead |citeseerx=10.1.1.5.9046}} See also: {{cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |last2=Woods |first2=John |date=2005 |orig-year=2003 |title=A Practical Logic of Cognitive Systems |location=Amsterdam; Boston |publisher=North-Holland |isbn=044451385X |oclc=52127672 |doi=10.1016/s1874-5075(03)x8001-8}}</ref>
